dossier.topic_summary: 把 LLM-as-a-judge 从『主观打分』推到『客观事实判定』时，核心瓶颈是 judge 的失败是沉默的：它会在没有参考答案的情况下自信地给出错误裁决。本期主角论文用『校准阈值 + 弃权 + 检索回退』把裁决变成一个有有限样本风险保证的过程：在留出集上用 Clopper–Pearson 区间校准阈值，使被接受裁决中的假阳性率(FDR)以高概率低于用户指定的 α，低置信实例路由到带网络证据的检索增强模式二次裁决。机制上它属于 Learn-then-Test / Conformal Risk Control 这一支风险控制谱系，但针对的是参考无关的二元正确/错误裁决。
dossier.beginner_context: 以前用 LLM 当裁判，主要是给『哪种回答更有帮助/更安全』这类主观题打分，因为没有一个标准答案，近似一致就够了。但如果你要它判断『这个回答的事实对不对』，情况完全不同：答案是二元的，而裁判既可能没学过相关知识，也可能产生幻觉，最危险的是这两种失败都不吭声——它照样给你一个很自信的裁决。现在卡住的点是：市面上 LLM 裁判没有一个机制能对『我接受的裁决里最多有多少比例是错的』给出可验证的保证，也没有统一的办法决定什么时候该花成本去查资料、什么时候干脆弃权。本周值得谈的正是第一篇把『有限样本的统计风险保证』装进 LLM 事实性裁判的工作，以及它的保证到底值多少钱。

reader_context.target_reader: 有软件或 AI 基础，但没有持续关注 LLM 评估与风险控制交叉方向

prerequisites.plain_definition: 用一个 LLM 对另一个模型生成的输出打分或给出对错/质量评判
prerequisites.why_needed: 这是全文要改造的对象，必须先知道裁判会怎么输出

prerequisites.concept: False discovery rate (FDR) / 被接受裁决的错误率
prerequisites.plain_definition: 在所有被系统『接受并当作结论』的裁决里，实际判错的比例
prerequisites.why_needed: 这是整篇论文要控制的量，不理解它就听不懂『保证』指什么

prerequisites.plain_definition: 只在高置信时给答案、低置信时拒绝回答，用覆盖率换错误率
prerequisites.why_needed: 弃权是控制 FDR 的唯一杠杆：不接受的裁决不计入风险

prerequisites.plain_definition: 对『n 次中成功 k 次』的二项比例给出精确(非渐近)置信区间的经典方法
prerequisites.why_needed: 它是把『在留出集上观测到的错误率』外推成『有限样本保证』的数学工具

prerequisites.concept: 可交换性 / 分布内假设(exchangeability)
prerequisites.plain_definition: 校准集与部署数据来自同一分布、顺序无关的假设，是保证成立的前提
prerequisites.why_needed: 决定『保证』何时失效——它是分布内的合同，不是跨分布保险
prerequisites.must_explain_before: 开放问题里的分布偏移讨论

causal_bridge: LLM 裁判在主观题上够用，但客观事实判定会遇到『自信地判错』的沉默失败，且没有参考标准答案可依赖
自然的解法是选择性预测：给每个裁决配一个置信度，低于阈值就弃权
但随手定的阈值没有统计保证——需要把阈值当成待校准参数，在留出集上用 Clopper–Pearson 上限界来挑一个『观测错误率的上界 ≤ α』的最不保守阈值
只靠参数化模式弃权会损失覆盖率，于是加第二级：不自信的实例路由到检索网络证据后重新裁决，用第二个校准阈值再守一道门
两级门合并统计后，被接受裁决的 FDR 依然以高概率 ≤ α（保证对路由机制无额外假设地成立）
但保证约束的是校准过程而非置信信号本身：若部署分布的置信度不能给错误排序，阈值会退化成『几乎全弃权』或跨分布静默超收
likely_reader_questions: 裁判的置信度分数到底怎么来的？是 token 概率、多次采样的自洽度，还是让模型口述的自信程度？
Clopper–Pearson 和 Learn-then-Test 用的 Hoeffding/Bentkus 不等式相比有什么差别？
如果第二级检索到的网络证据本身是错的或误导性的，两级路由的 FDR 保证还成立吗？
换了领域（新实体、新事件）之后，这个保证还会不会兑现？
为什么说『基于不确定性的弃权』应该比『随机弃权』在相同 FDR 下覆盖率更高，这个优势有没有被原文直接验证？

dossier.core_intuition: 把『LLM 裁判的可靠性』从『模型能力问题』改写成『统计过程控制问题』：你不需要让裁判永远对，只需要把它每次裁决附带的置信度当作一条风险-覆盖率曲线，然后用 Clopper–Pearson 区间在留出集上给这条曲线标刻度，选出能证伪『FDR ≤ α』的最宽松阈值。心智模型是工厂质检的抽检上限：『我抽查了 n 个被接受的裁决、错 k 个，Clopper–Pearson 说真实错误率几乎不可能超过某个上界』——这个上界是有限样本的、精确的，不靠渐近正态近似。所以问题的正确切法是：先保证『被接受的裁决里错误比例有界』（统计合同），再用检索回退来救覆盖率（经济杠杆），两者解耦。
dossier.running_example: 一家公司用 LLM 裁判自动复核 10,000 条 AI 生成的开放域问答（例：『哪家公司最先发布商用量子计算机？』候选答案为某公司+某年份），要求：被自动接受、不送人工复核的裁决里，最多 5% 可以是错的，同时希望尽量少花钱送人工。这个场景贯穿全文：参数化裁判会答、检索裁判能查网络、弃权则把人送人工。观察指标始终是两条：覆盖率（10,000 条里被自动接受的比例）与被接受集合的 FDR（判错比例）。
dossier.primary_work_title: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain: Uncertainty-Guarded LLM Judging with Provable Risk Guarantees

key_works.title: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain: Uncertainty-Guarded LLM Judging with Provable Risk Guarantees
key_works.why_relevant: 本期主角：第一篇在参考无关的客观事实判定场景里，把 LLM 裁判的弃权/检索动作与有限样本 FDR 上界绑定，而非只报告经验准确率。
key_works.key_findings: （以下均来自已抓取的全文摘要与引言，方法细节的全文截断处未覆盖，需在写作阶段核对方法节）(1) 框架在留出校准集上校准不确定性阈值，使『被接受裁决的 FDR』以高概率不超过用户指定 α，工具是有限样本 Clopper–Pearson 区间；(2) 分两种模式：参数化模式（无参考、靠模型参数知识判事实对错）与检索增强模式（抓取网络证据后重新裁决）；(3) 参数化模式置信不足时，实例被路由到检索增强模式，在第二个校准阈值下再裁决，否则弃权；(4) 有限样本保证对两级路由成立且无需额外假设；(5) 在开放域 QA 基准与不同规模 judge 上，维持目标错误率同时覆盖率显著高于单模式基线。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 对 10,000 条复核任务：每条先走参数化裁判拿一个置信度，超过第一阈值 τ₁ 的直接接受；低于 τ₁ 的（比如『2023 年后的新公司/新产品』这类模型知识可能过期的题）自动转检索网络证据再判，超过第二阈值 τ₂ 才接受，两关都不达标的送人工。可观察差异是：相比只跑参数化裁判或只跑检索裁判的单模式基线，它在把被接受集合 FDR 压到 5% 的同时接受了更大比例的任务（更高覆盖率），且这个 5% 上限是留出集上校准出来的有限样本保证，不是事后经验值。

key_works.title: Learn then Test: Calibrating Predictive Algorithms to Achieve Risk Control
key_works.why_relevant: 机制祖先是它：把风险控制重构为多重假设检验，用校准数据给任意黑盒模型盖有限样本保证的章，是『在留出集上校准阈值使 FDR ≤ α』的直接出处。
key_works.key_findings: （来自已抓取全文）(1) 核心洞见是把风险控制问题改写成多重假设检验，用固定序列检验(fixed sequence testing)在候选阈值中认证一个 λ̂，使预测集合的 FDR 有界（如多标签分类 ≤10%）；(2) 对模型内部与数据分布不做假设、无需重训，只需校准数据后处理；(3) 给出 FDR（多标签分类）、实例分割 IoU、离群检测一类错误与分类回归覆盖率同时控制等工作示例；(4) 框架是有限样本保证，不依赖渐近。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 在复核场景里它扮演『参数化模式的第一道门』：把裁判置信度当作分数、把阈值 λ 当作待认证参数，在校准集上固定序列地测试各候选 λ，认证出 FDR ≤ 5% 的最宽松 λ̂。但 LTT 原文没有检索回退——低置信实例只能被直接弃权，因此覆盖率会随 α 收紧而掉得很快；这正是本期论文补的第二级路由所解决的问题。

key_works.title: Explicit Abstention Knobs for Predictable Reliability in Video Question Answering
key_works.why_relevant: 正面回答了本期要验证的『随机弃权 vs 不确定性弃权』：证实置信度阈值在分布内给出平滑的 risk-coverage 机械控制，但揭示保证是『分布内合同』——证据退化时置信度不收缩，模型『不知道自己不知道』。
key_works.key_findings: （来自已抓取全文，NExT-QA + Gemini 2.0 Flash）(1) 分布内：扫阈值 ε 得到平滑 risk-coverage 曲线，错误率从 23.6% 降到 9.4%（覆盖率 63.7%），预测校准良好 ECE=0.018；(2) 证据退化（18 帧减到 6 帧）下，同一批问题两种证据条件的 self-reported 置信度中位数都停在 0.9，尽管视觉信息减少 3 倍；(3) 用单独提示接口取的 logprob 置信度 p_max 表现出同样的失效模式；(4) 结论：模型不能『知道自己不知道』，由此提出 warrant-based 选择性预测（置信度必须被证据所能支撑的程度显式约束）。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 如果复核任务突然涌入裁判训练数据之后才出现的新产品/新事件，该论文的教训是：裁判的置信度可能仍停留在 0.9 附近、不发出弃权信号，于是用留出集校准出的 τ 会照常接受大量实例，实际 FDR 静默越过 5%——Clopper–Pearson 上界只在留出集与部署同分布时才兑现。这正是对本期论文『保证无需额外假设地延续到两级路由』的反向注脚：数学上路由成立，但置信信号在偏移下失效。

key_works.title: Analyzing Uncertainty of LLM-as-a-Judge: Interval Evaluations with Conformal Prediction
key_works.why_relevant: 同一年、同一方向但目标不同的近邻工作：用 conformal prediction 给 LLM 裁判的打分输出预测区间，提供覆盖率保证——与本期论文的二元 FDR 控制互补，帮读者区分『评分的不确定区间』与『裁决的风险控制』。
key_works.key_findings: （来自已抓取全文）(1) 提出首个用 conformal prediction 分析 LLM-as-a-judge 不确定性的框架，从单次评估构造连续预测区间，并设计 ordinal boundary adjustment 处理离散评级；(2) 区间中点比原始模型分更低偏；(3) 综合评估 9 种 conformal 方法（7 回归型 + 2 序数型），度量效率（区间平均宽度）与覆盖率；(4) 保证来自可交换性下的 conformal coverage guarantee。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 它不直接给出『接受/弃权』的二元决策，而是给每条复核任务输出一个评分区间（例如正确性评分 3.2–4.1）。在本期场景里它回答的是『这个分数有多稳』，而主角论文回答的是『我接受的裁决里错的比例能否有界』——两者是同一裁判的不同不确定性接口，写作时可用它做对照而非替代。

key_works.title: Conformal Risk Control
key_works.why_relevant: 把 conformal 的覆盖率保证推广到任意单调有界损失的期望控制，是 FDR 控制更一般的理论容器；也提供了与 Clopper–Pearson『高概率界』相对的『期望界』视角。
key_works.key_findings: （来自已抓取全文）(1) 扩展 conformal prediction 到控制任意单调损失期望 E[ℓ(C(X),Y)] ≤ α，当 ℓ 随预测集变大而缩小时成立；(2) 过程紧到 O(1/n)；(3) 覆盖 miscoverage、FNR、F1 等工作示例；(4) 提出对分布偏移、分位数风险控制、多重与对抗风险控制、U-统计量期望的扩展。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 在复核场景里，若把『被接受集合的 FDR』写成随接受阈值单调的损失函数，CRC 可给出 FDR 的期望界；主角论文选择 Clopper–Pearson 则给的是『以高概率』的有限样本界。这一区别影响保证的口径（高概率 vs 期望），也是写作时值得点出的机制分叉：高概率界更保守、更贴近『单次部署』的直觉。

background_notes.point: LLM-as-a-judge 已成规模化评估标准做法，主要用于主观/开放式任务（helpfulness、alignment），并已知存在位置偏差、冗长偏好、自我增强等偏差。
该方向有系统综述，明确区分了主观打分与客观/事实性判定的不同可靠性要求。
客观事实判定中 judge 的失败是『沉默的』：知识边界与幻觉都可能导致高置信的错误裁决，且无参考答案可依赖。
Clopper–Pearson 区间是对二项比例『n 中成功 k 次』给出精确有限样本置信区间的经典统计方法，这正是论文能给出高概率 FDR 界的来源。
Learn-then-Test 把风险控制改写为多重假设检验，用固定序列检验认证阈值，给出有限样本 FDR 保证；是本期校准机制的谱系祖先。
Conformal Risk Control 将保证推广到任意单调有界损失的期望控制，紧到 O(1/n)，并含分布偏移扩展——是『期望界』路线的代表。
选择性预测的核心是 risk-coverage 曲线：置信度阈值应产生平滑、单调的错误率-覆盖率权衡；随机弃权在这条曲线上没有选择性优势（FDR 恒等于基线错误率）。
参考无关的检索增强评估已有先例（如 Ragas 对 RAG 管线做无参考评估），但未提供被接受裁决的统计风险控制。
LLM 裁判对呈现顺序敏感（listwise 判事实性时答案顺序可改变裁决），是另一种与置信度无关的裁判不稳定性来源。

open_questions: 裁判置信度的具体来源未在已抓取的全文片段中披露（token 概率、多次采样自洽度、还是口述置信度）。不同的信号在分布偏移下失效方式不同（视频 QA 研究显示 self-reported 与 logprob p_max 都『不知道自己不知道』），写作前必须核对方法节确认其 UQ 信号并检查是否有跨分布验证。
有限样本 FDR 保证的可交换性假设在部署中极易被打破：Abstention Knobs 论文证明置信度在证据退化下不收缩、阈值静默超收；主角论文声称保证对两级路由『无需额外假设』，但那是路由统计的数学性质，不等于置信信号在偏移数据上仍有区分度——'保证能否跨分布兑现'是未解决的争议点。
『不确定性弃权在相同 FDR 下覆盖率高于随机弃权』这一 thesis 成分没有被原文直接验证（原文的对比对象是单模式基线，非随机弃权）；它依赖『置信度能给错误排序』这一前提，而该前提在分布内成立、在偏移下可能崩塌，需由计划中的复现实验在客观 QA 集上实测确认。
dossier.narrative_angle: 读者应带走的世界模型更新是：LLM 裁判的可靠性问题，已经从『能不能让裁判更准』被切成了『能不能给被接受的裁决一份有限样本的统计合同』——Clopper–Pearson 校准把阈值从一个调参旋钮变成可证明的旋钮（被接受集合的 FDR 以高概率 ≤ α），两级路由则用『只在不确定处花检索预算』来救覆盖率，二者解耦后保证自然延续。但这张合同写的是分布内条款：它保证的是校准过程的正确性，不保证置信信号本身有区分度。一旦部署分布漂移、裁判『自信地错』，合同照签、FDR 照破——所以真正该追问的不是『能不能界住 FDR』，而是『裁判的置信度是否足够有信息量，让这个界能换来覆盖率而不是换来全量弃权』。这也是为什么随机弃权 vs 不确定性弃权的对照实验比论文主打的单模式对照更锋利：它直接测的是置信信号的选择性价值，而不是框架的统计正确性。

mechanism_cards.problem: 在无参考的客观事实判定场景中，使用LLM作为裁判评估QA答案正确性时，裁判可能因参数知识缺失或幻觉给出错误但自信的裁决；现有选择性评估方法只采用弃权，没有提供路由到检索的机制，并且缺乏对已接受裁决错误率的正式统计保证。
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：问题-答案对（QA实例）。输出：三类动作之一——接受裁决（正确/错误）、路由到检索增强模式后接受裁决、弃权并转人工审查。用户指定风险参数：目标FDR α、置信水平（高概率）δ。
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 校准阶段存储两个阈值：τ1（模式1接受阈值）、τ2（模式2接受阈值），以及留出校准集上的裁决、不确定性分数和真实标签。推理阶段每个实例维护状态：当前模式（1或2）、裁决结果、不确定性分数、是否已检索、最终是否接受/弃权。关键接口：模式1的不确定性估计器（输出置信度或不确定性分数）、模式2的网络检索工具（输入问题-答案对，输出相关证据）、裁判模型接口（输入问题-答案对及可选证据，输出裁决和不确定性）。原文未给出具体数据结构或API签名。
algorithm_steps: 在留出校准集上，对每个实例执行模式1裁判，获得裁决和不确定性分数；结合真实标签，通过Clopper–Pearson上置信界，联合校准两个阈值τ1和τ2，使得在固定阈值对下FDR≤α的概率至少为1-δ。
对每个新QA实例，先进入模式1：裁判仅依据参数化知识输出裁决及不确定性分数；若该分数满足模式1接受条件（即不超过τ1），则接受该裁决并输出。
若模式1不确定性分数不满足接受条件，将实例路由到模式2：调用网络检索工具获取相关证据，将证据并入上下文，裁判重新评估并输出新的裁决及不确定性分数。
在模式2中，若新的不确定性分数满足模式2接受条件（即不超过τ2），则接受该裁决并输出；否则裁判弃权，将该实例标记为人工审查。
所有被接受的裁决构成最终预测集；由于阈值校准，该集合的FDR以高概率不超过用户指定α。

evidence.claim: 框架在留出集上校准不确定性阈值，使已接受裁决的FDR以高概率不超过用户指定α，使用有限样本Clopper–Pearson区间。
当参数化模式不够自信时，实例被路由到检索增强模式，裁判收集网络证据并在第二个校准阈值下重新评估。
如果裁判在检索后仍不确定，则弃权并将实例标记为人工审查。
有限样本FDR保证在无额外假设的情况下延伸到双阈值路由设置。
实验在开放域QA基准和不同规模裁判上，保持目标错误率，同时覆盖率显著高于单模式基线。
两个阈值在具有已知ground-truth标签的留出集上通过Clopper–Pearson上置信界联合校准。

failure_modes: 模式1可能因知识缺失或幻觉给出高置信但错误的裁决，若未触发路由条件，则错误被接受。
模式2检索可能无法找到相关或有用证据，导致裁决仍不确定而弃权，降低覆盖率。

检索到的网络证据本身可能包含错误或虚假信息，但框架未处理证据可信度。
limits: 仅适用于客观事实QA的二元正确/错误评估，不适用于主观、开放生成任务。
需要带真实标签的留出集进行阈值校准，实际中可能成本较高或不可得。
引入网络检索增加额外计算开销和推理延迟。
双阈值校准保证的是已接受裁决的FDR，而非提高所有实例的整体准确率。

mechanism_cards.problem: 为任意预训练模型后处理，通过校准数据选择低维参数 λ，使最终预测的风险（用户选定的统计错误率）以有限样本保证控制在 α 以下（概率≥1−δ）。核心是将风险控制重构为多重假设检验。
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：预训练模型 f̂: 𝒳→𝒵，i.i.d. 校准集 (Xi,Yi)i=1,...,n，用户选择风险容忍 α、错误水平 δ，参数候选空间 Λ 与后处理映射 𝒯λ: 𝒳→𝒴′，风险函数 R(𝒯λ)（简记 R(λ)）。输出：选定的参数 λ̂∈Λ 及预测 𝒯_{λ̂}，满足 ℙ(R(𝒯_{λ̂})≤α)≥1−δ；若该风险在某些分布/水平下无法控制，则返回弃权。
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 校准数据 (Xi,Yi)；预训练模型 f̂ 输出空间 𝒵；后处理映射 𝒯λ；低维参数 λ∈Λ；风险函数 R(λ)；候选 λ 在固定序列检验中被逐一测试。多标签分类例：f̂: 𝒳→[0,1]^K，𝒯λ(x)={k: f̂(x)_k ≥ λ}。
algorithm_steps: 使用预训练模型 f̂，准备 i.i.d. 校准集 {(Xi,Yi)}。
定义参数化的后处理映射 𝒯λ: 𝒳→𝒴′ 和风险函数 R(𝒯λ)（或简写 R(λ)），风险对应要控制的统计错误率。
在校准数据上测试多个候选 λ 值（固定序列检验），寻找能够控制风险的 λ̂。
若找到满足 ℙ(R(𝒯_{λ̂})≤α)≥1−δ 的 λ̂，返回 𝒯_{λ̂}；否则弃权。

evidence.claim: LTT 将风险控制问题重构为多重假设检验。
校准算法适用于任意底层模型和未知数据生成分布，且无需模型重训。
LTT 提供有限样本保证，不依赖渐近。
(α,δ)-风险控制预测定义为 ℙ(R(𝒯_{λ̂})≤α)≥1−δ。
框架支持多标签分类 FDR 控制、实例分割 IoU 控制、离群检测一类错误与分类/回归置信集覆盖率的同时控制。
以往分布无关不确定性量化方法要求 λ 一维且风险单调；LTT 不作这些假设。
多标签分类示例中，使用固定序列检验可认证 λ̂ 使 FDR≤10%。
某些风险不能在所有 α 水平及所有数据生成分布下被控制，此时选择弃权。

failure_modes: 某些风险在特定数据分布或 α 水平下无法控制，算法会弃权而不返回 RCP。
若固定序列检验未能在候选 λ 中找到满足风险控制的参数，则无法给出保证（对应弃权）。

mechanism_cards.problem: 高风险视频问答中，基于置信度的弃权是否提供可靠的错误率控制，并在证据质量退化（帧数减少）下是否保持可靠；具体诊断置信度阈值在分布内提供机制控制但缺乏认知有效性（不能知道自己不知道）。
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：视频问答实例（NExT-QA 问题与视频帧，证据条件可为18帧或6帧）。输出：模型预测答案和置信度分数（self-reported confidence 或 logprob-derived p_max）；在阈值扫描下输出风险-覆盖率曲线及覆盖率、错误率、校准误差（ECE）。
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 关键状态：每个问题实例的预测答案、置信度分数；全局阈值 ε；以及由阈值决定的接受/弃权决策和统计指标（覆盖率、错误率）。读写：模型（Gemini 2.0 Flash）生成预测与置信度；选择机制读取置信度并与 ε 比较决定是否回答；评估器读取真实标签计算指标。接口：模型推理 API（未具体命名）；logprob 置信度通过单独 prompt interface 获取。原文未提供具体数据结构或 API 细节。
algorithm_steps: 为每个视频问答实例准备输入：从视频中采样指定帧数（18帧或6帧）作为视觉证据，并附带问题文本。
对每个实例，调用 Gemini 2.0 Flash 模型取得预测答案和 self-reported confidence；若需要 logprob p_max 变体，则使用单独的提示接口获取模型对答案 token 的最大概率。
在分布内（18帧全证据）扫描阈值 ε 从低到高（例如0到1），对每个 ε：若置信度≥ε 则接受该预测，否则弃权。
对每个 ε，计算覆盖率（被接受的实例比例）和错误率（被接受实例中预测错误的比例），绘制 risk-coverage 曲线；记录典型操作点：98.7%覆盖率时23.6%错误，63.7%覆盖率时9.4%错误。
计算分布内预测的校准误差（ECE）以验证置信度校准程度。
对同一批冻结问题实例，在6帧证据条件下重复步骤1-4获取置信度和风险-覆盖率数据。
比较两种证据条件下的置信度分布（例如中位数 self-reported confidence 和 logprob p_max），检查是否随证据减少而下降。

evidence.claim: 在分布内，扫描阈值 ε 产生平滑的风险-覆盖率权衡，错误率从23.6%降至9.4%（覆盖率63.7%），预测校准良好（ECE=0.018）。
在证据退化（18帧减到6帧）下，同一批问题的 self-reported confidence 中位数保持0.9，尽管视觉信息减少3倍。
通过单独提示接口获取的 logprob-derived confidence p_max 表现出与 self-reported confidence 相同的失效模式。
模型在证据偏移下不能“知道自己不知道”，这促使提出基于证据许可的置信度约束（warrant-based selective prediction）。

failure_modes: 证据退化下，置信度分布收缩不足，中位数保持0.9，模型不能知道自己不知道。
self-reported confidence 与 logprob p_max 都无法跟踪信息可用性。
在证据退化时，原先调优的阈值不能保持相同的覆盖率：同样的9%错误率只对应53.7%覆盖率，而全证据下为63.7%。
limits: 仅针对视频问答，使用 NExT-QA 和 Gemini 2.0 Flash，可能不推广到其他模型/任务。
仅考察一种证据退化类型（帧数减少）；未探索其他分布偏移（如低分辨率、压缩等）。
未实现或验证 warrant-based selective prediction 方法，仅指出需求。
未提供对风险-覆盖率曲线单调性的严格统计检验。
gaps: 原文未描述模型内部置信度的具体计算方式或提示模板。
未提供具体 API 名称、数据结构或存储方案。
未给出阈值扫描的具体范围或步长。
未说明 ECE 的计算方法细节。

mechanism_cards.problem: LLM-as-a-judge 的单次评分可能因固有随机性而存在偏差和不确定性，缺乏可靠性；尤其在医疗、金融等高风险场景中，直接使用单次打分风险较高。该工作要解决如何为 LLM 裁判的评分输出提供可靠的不确定量化，即给出具有覆盖率保证的预测区间。
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：用户给出的评估请求（文本/自然语言生成任务），由 LLM judge 进行一次评分，得到原始 rating。输出：针对该 rating 的 prediction interval（连续区间，可经序数边界调整对齐到离散评级刻度），以及可选的 interval midpoint 作为低偏差点估计。评估阶段还输出 efficiency（区间平均宽度）和 coverage（真值落入区间的比例）。
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 关键接口/状态：LLM-as-judge 黑盒模型，接受评估文本并输出 rating；conformal prediction 需要 calibration data（基于 LLM 输出进行校准）来构造区间；输出为 prediction interval（连续/经边界调整对齐评级尺度）及可选 midpoint。原文摘要/引言未给出具体 conformity score、数据结构或 API 签名，因此无法提供更细粒度的状态表示。
algorithm_steps: 接收用户评估请求，调用 LLM judge 进行一次评分（single evaluation run），得到原始 rating 输出。
从 9 种 conformal prediction 方法中选择一种（7 种回归型或 2 种序数型），利用 calibration data 基于 LLM 输出进行校准，构造连续 prediction interval。
若评分任务是离散评级，应用 ordinal boundary adjustment：将 prediction interval 的端点调整到与 rating scale 对齐（例如映射到有效评级刻度），使区间适合序数/离散输出；该方法被证明在覆盖率上非递减。
输出最终 prediction interval；可选地取该 interval 的 midpoint 作为低偏差点估计，替代 raw model score 或 weighted average。
可选评估步骤：计算 interval 的平均宽度作为 efficiency、ground truth 落入 interval 的比例作为 coverage，并分析校准集大小、LLM judge 选择与 prompting 策略等因素对区间质量的影响。

evidence.claim: 该工作首次使用 conformal prediction 分析 LLM-as-a-judge 在 rating-based evaluation 中的不确定性。
Conformal prediction 从单次评估运行构造连续预测区间。
针对离散评级任务设计了 ordinal boundary adjustment，将区间端点调整到与 rating scale 对齐，且覆盖率非递减。
区间中点作为低偏分数，优于原始模型分和加权平均。
综合评估了 9 种 conformal prediction 方法（7 种回归型、2 种序数型），并报告 efficiency（区间平均宽度）与 coverage。
在可交换性假设下，conformal prediction 可以提供具有统计覆盖保证的有效预测区间。
用预测区间重新提示 LLM judge（reprompting）可能不会改善判断。

mechanism_cards.problem: 将 split conformal prediction 的误覆盖率控制（E[1{Y∉C(X)}]≤α）推广为控制任意单调有界损失的期望风险 E[ℓ(C_λ(X),Y)]≤α，并给出紧至 O(1/n) 的有限样本保证。
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：校准数据 {(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1}^n，参数化后处理函数 C_λ(·)，损失函数 ℓ 满足 ℓ(C_λ(x),y)∈(-∞,B] 且对 λ 非增，目标风险上界 α∈(-∞,B)。输出：阈值 λ̂∈Λ，用于部署 C_{λ̂}(·)；等价地，在抽象形式中输入为可交换非增随机函数 L_i:Λ→(-∞,B], i=1,...,n+1，输出为 λ̂，使 E[L_{n+1}(λ̂)]≤α。
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 保留每条校准样本的损失函数 L_i(λ)（或可实时求值），用于计算经验风险 R̂_n(λ)=(1/n)∑_{i=1}^n L_i(λ)；选定 λ̂ 后作为部署参数。关键接口：λ̂=inf{λ: n/(n+1)R̂_n(λ)+B/(n+1)≤α}；C_λ(x) 由基础模型 f 的输出后处理得到，λ 增大使输出更保守；对于连续 Λ，原文未指定离散化/搜索实现。
algorithm_steps: 对每个校准样本 i=1,...,n，构造（或求值）损失函数 L_i(λ)=ℓ(C_λ(X_i),Y_i)，并确认 L_i(λ) 对 λ 非增。
对候选 λ∈Λ 计算经验风险 R̂_n(λ)=(1/n)∑_{i=1}^n L_i(λ)。
计算调整风险值 D(λ)=n/(n+1)R̂_n(λ)+B/(n+1)。
选择 λ̂=inf{λ∈Λ:D(λ)≤α}；若集合为空，则设 λ̂=λ_max=sup Λ。
对新测试点 X_{n+1} 部署 λ̂，输出 C_{λ̂}(X_{n+1})。

evidence.claim: 算法保证期望风险控制 E[L_{n+1}(λ̂)]≤α。
λ̂ 由方程 λ̂=inf{λ: n/(n+1)R̂_n(λ)+B/(n+1)≤α} 定义，空集时取 λ_max。
损失函数需非增，且值域上界为 B<∞。
当 L_i 为 i.i.d. 且来自连续分布时，算法满足下界 E[L_{n+1}(λ̂)]≥α-2B/(n+1)。
若风险非单调，则该算法不控制风险。
该过程紧至 O(1/n) 因子。
在 miscoverage loss ℓ(C(X),Y)=1{Y∉C(X)} 下，恢复 conformal miscoverage guarantee。

mechanism_cards.title: Conformal Risk Control

high_mechanism_cards.problem: 在无参考的客观事实判定场景中，使用LLM作为裁判评估QA答案正确性时，裁判可能因参数知识缺失或幻觉给出错误但自信的裁决；现有选择性评估方法只采用弃权，没有提供路由到检索的机制，并且缺乏对已接受裁决错误率的正式统计保证。
high_mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：问题-答案对（QA实例）。输出：三类动作之一——接受裁决（正确/错误）、路由到检索增强模式后接受裁决、弃权并转人工审查。用户指定风险参数：目标FDR α、置信水平（高概率）δ。
high_mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 校准阶段存储两个阈值：τ1（模式1接受阈值）、τ2（模式2接受阈值），以及留出校准集上的裁决、不确定性分数和真实标签。推理阶段每个实例维护状态：当前模式（1或2）、裁决结果、不确定性分数、是否已检索、最终是否接受/弃权。关键接口：模式1的不确定性估计器（输出置信度或不确定性分数）、模式2的网络检索工具（输入问题-答案对，输出相关证据）、裁判模型接口（输入问题-答案对及可选证据，输出裁决和不确定性）。原文未给出具体数据结构或API签名。
algorithm_steps: 在留出校准集上，对每个实例执行模式1裁判，获得裁决和不确定性分数；结合真实标签，通过Clopper–Pearson上置信界，联合校准两个阈值τ1和τ2，使得在固定阈值对下FDR≤α的概率至少为1-δ。
对每个新QA实例，先进入模式1：裁判仅依据参数化知识输出裁决及不确定性分数；若该分数满足模式1接受条件（即不超过τ1），则接受该裁决并输出。
若模式1不确定性分数不满足接受条件，将实例路由到模式2：调用网络检索工具获取相关证据，将证据并入上下文，裁判重新评估并输出新的裁决及不确定性分数。
在模式2中，若新的不确定性分数满足模式2接受条件（即不超过τ2），则接受该裁决并输出；否则裁判弃权，将该实例标记为人工审查。
所有被接受的裁决构成最终预测集；由于阈值校准，该集合的FDR以高概率不超过用户指定α。

evidence.claim: 框架在留出集上校准不确定性阈值，使已接受裁决的FDR以高概率不超过用户指定α，使用有限样本Clopper–Pearson区间。
当参数化模式不够自信时，实例被路由到检索增强模式，裁判收集网络证据并在第二个校准阈值下重新评估。
如果裁判在检索后仍不确定，则弃权并将实例标记为人工审查。
有限样本FDR保证在无额外假设的情况下延伸到双阈值路由设置。
实验在开放域QA基准和不同规模裁判上，保持目标错误率，同时覆盖率显著高于单模式基线。
两个阈值在具有已知ground-truth标签的留出集上通过Clopper–Pearson上置信界联合校准。

failure_modes: 模式1可能因知识缺失或幻觉给出高置信但错误的裁决，若未触发路由条件，则错误被接受。
模式2检索可能无法找到相关或有用证据，导致裁决仍不确定而弃权，降低覆盖率。

检索到的网络证据本身可能包含错误或虚假信息，但框架未处理证据可信度。

需要带真实标签的留出集进行阈值校准，实际中可能成本较高或不可得。
引入网络检索增加额外计算开销和推理延迟。
双阈值校准保证的是已接受裁决的FDR，而非提高所有实例的整体准确率。

high_mechanism_cards.problem: 高风险视频问答中，基于置信度的弃权是否提供可靠的错误率控制，并在证据质量退化（帧数减少）下是否保持可靠；具体诊断置信度阈值在分布内提供机制控制但缺乏认知有效性（不能知道自己不知道）。
high_mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：视频问答实例（NExT-QA 问题与视频帧，证据条件可为18帧或6帧）。输出：模型预测答案和置信度分数（self-reported confidence 或 logprob-derived p_max）；在阈值扫描下输出风险-覆盖率曲线及覆盖率、错误率、校准误差（ECE）。
high_mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 关键状态：每个问题实例的预测答案、置信度分数；全局阈值 ε；以及由阈值决定的接受/弃权决策和统计指标（覆盖率、错误率）。读写：模型（Gemini 2.0 Flash）生成预测与置信度；选择机制读取置信度并与 ε 比较决定是否回答；评估器读取真实标签计算指标。接口：模型推理 API（未具体命名）；logprob 置信度通过单独 prompt interface 获取。原文未提供具体数据结构或 API 细节。
algorithm_steps: 为每个视频问答实例准备输入：从视频中采样指定帧数（18帧或6帧）作为视觉证据，并附带问题文本。
对每个实例，调用 Gemini 2.0 Flash 模型取得预测答案和 self-reported confidence；若需要 logprob p_max 变体，则使用单独的提示接口获取模型对答案 token 的最大概率。
在分布内（18帧全证据）扫描阈值 ε 从低到高（例如0到1），对每个 ε：若置信度≥ε 则接受该预测，否则弃权。
对每个 ε，计算覆盖率（被接受的实例比例）和错误率（被接受实例中预测错误的比例），绘制 risk-coverage 曲线；记录典型操作点：98.7%覆盖率时23.6%错误，63.7%覆盖率时9.4%错误。
计算分布内预测的校准误差（ECE）以验证置信度校准程度。
对同一批冻结问题实例，在6帧证据条件下重复步骤1-4获取置信度和风险-覆盖率数据。
比较两种证据条件下的置信度分布（例如中位数 self-reported confidence 和 logprob p_max），检查是否随证据减少而下降。

evidence.claim: 在分布内，扫描阈值 ε 产生平滑的风险-覆盖率权衡，错误率从23.6%降至9.4%（覆盖率63.7%），预测校准良好（ECE=0.018）。
在证据退化（18帧减到6帧）下，同一批问题的 self-reported confidence 中位数保持0.9，尽管视觉信息减少3倍。
通过单独提示接口获取的 logprob-derived confidence p_max 表现出与 self-reported confidence 相同的失效模式。
模型在证据偏移下不能“知道自己不知道”，这促使提出基于证据许可的置信度约束（warrant-based selective prediction）。

self-reported confidence 与 logprob p_max 都无法跟踪信息可用性。
在证据退化时，原先调优的阈值不能保持相同的覆盖率：同样的9%错误率只对应53.7%覆盖率，而全证据下为63.7%。

evidence.title: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain: Uncertainty-Guarded LLM Judging with Provable Risk Guarantees
evidence.excerpt: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain: Uncertainty-Guarded LLM Judging with Provable Risk Guarantees Sher Badshah Affiliation: Dalhousie University Affiliation: New York University Abu Dhabi Ali Emami Affiliation: Emory University {sh545346,hsajjad}@dal.caali.emami@emory.edu Hassan Sajjad Affiliation: Dalhousie University Affiliation: New York University Abu Dhabi Abstract Using LLMs as judges has become standard practice for evaluating model outputs at scale. This is particularly common for subjective, open-ended tasks such as assessing helpfulness or alignment, where no single reference answer exists. However, objective tasks introduce a distinct reliability challenge for reference-free LLM judging. In the absence of a reference answer, the judge evaluates factual correctness either through its parametric knowledge or through tool augmentation. Although the former enables efficient evaluation, the judge may hallucinate or lack sufficient evidence for its verdict. Conversely, tool augmentation can provide additional evidence but introduces extra computational cost and requires an appropriate mechanism to determine when and how that evidence should be used reliably. More importantly, neither approach alone provides formal control over the risk of accepted verdicts or guarantees their reliability at a specified level. We propose a risk-controlled framework that calibrates uncertainty thresholds on a held-out set so that the false discovery rate among accepted verdicts remains below a user-specified level α \alpha with high probability, using finite-sample Clopper–Pearson intervals. When the parametric mode is not sufficiently confident, the instance is routed to a retrieval-augmented mode, where the judge gathers web evidence and re-evaluates the instance under a second calibrated threshold. The finite-sample guarantee carries over to this two-threshold routing without additional assumptions. Across open-domain QA benchmarks and judges of varying scales, the framework maintains the target error rate while achieving substantially higher coverage than single-mode baselines. 1 Introduction LLM-as-a-judge has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation for assessing language model outputs ( 39 ) . It enables practitioners to evaluate thousands of model outputs at a fraction of the cost and time required for human annotation ( 11 ; 29 ) . However, most existing work employs LLM judges for subjective evaluation ( 6 ) , such as scoring outputs for helpfulness, harmlessness, or style in reward modeling, where no single correct answer exists and approximate agreement suffices ( 38 ; 19 ) . Extending LLM-as-a-judge to objective, factual evaluation remains an open challenge. In factual and open-domain QA, answers are either correct or incorrect, and the judge must make this determination reliably. However, obtaining ground-truth annotations for this purpose is expensive at scale ( 9 ; 22 ) , requires domain expertise for specialized questions, and is entirely infeasible when LLMs operate as autonomous agents answering open-ended queries in real-world environments where no pre-collected labels exist. LLM-as-a-judge offers a reference-free alternative that eliminates this dependency. Nevertheless, utilizing LLM judges to assess correctness without explicit references introduces two key reliability challenges ( 26 ; 7 ) . First, LLM judges are bounded by their training data and may lack knowledge of recent events, rare entities, or specialized domains ( 36 ) . Such limitations can prevent reliable distinction between correct answers and plausible fabrications. Second, even if the judge has the relevant knowledge, hallucinations may still cause it to produce confident but incorrect verdicts ( 12 ) . In both cases, the failures are silent as the judge provides no indication that its verdict is unreliable. Without a mechanism to quantify and act on this uncertainty, incorrect evaluations can propagate undetected into downstream decisions. Selective evaluation provides a natural mitigation strategy by allowing the judge to abstain when uncertain and produce a verdict only when it is likely to be correct. Uncertainty quantification methods can identify unreliable verdicts ( 27 ) . However, applying a heuristic threshold to these scores provides no formal guarantee on the error rate among accepted evaluations ( 5 ) . Recent work on risk-controlled selective prediction addresses this gap by calibrating statistically valid thresholds that bound the False Discovery Rate (FDR) among selected outputs with high probability ( 30 ; 33 ) . However, existing methods are designed to filter examinee answers in Question-Answering (QA) tasks rather than control errors in a meta-evaluation setting. Moreover, earlier methods treat abstention as the only recourse for uncertain instances. This discards cases where the judge’s uncertainty stems from a knowledge gap or hallucination that could be resolved with additional evidence ( 4 ) . In this paper, we propose a risk-controlled selective evaluation framework for LLM-as-a-judge that addresses the above limitations. Inspired by LLM-based agents that leverage external tools to overcome their parametric limitations, we equip the judge with web search as a tool to bridge its knowledge gaps. Our framework operates in two modes. In Mode 1, the judge model evaluates using only its parametric knowledge without any tool-augmentation. If the judge is confident, the verdict is accepted. If uncertain, the instance is routed to Mode 2 where the judge retrieves relevant evidence from the web and re-evaluates with this augmented context. If the judge remains uncertain after retrieval, it abstains and flags the instance for human review. Both thresholds are jointly calibrated on a held-out set with known ground-truth labels via Clopper–Pearson upper confidence bounds ( 10 ) . We prove that the finite-sample FDR guarantee for a fixed threshold pair extends to the two-threshold routing setting without additional distributional assumptions. Our contributions are: • We formulate risk-controlled selective evaluation for LLM-as-a-judge on factual QA. • We introduce a two-mode routing mechanism that equips the judge with adaptive web retrieval to resolve uncertainty before resorting to abstention. • We show that the Bernoulli structure required for the Clopper–Pearson bound extends to the two-threshold routing setting. • Experiments across open-domain QA benchmarks and judges of varying scales demonstrate that adaptive retrieval recovers substantial coverage over single-mode baselines while controlling the judge’s error rate. 2 Related Work LLM-as-a-Judge. Using LLMs to evaluate the outputs of other models has gained widespread adoption as a cost-effective alternative to human annotation. Strong LLMs can approximate human preferences on subjective dimensions ( 19 ) . As a result, they have been adopted for reward modeling and reinforcement learning ( 28 ) . More recently, LLM judges have been extended to objective tasks such as factual evaluation. SAFE ( 35 ) uses an LLM agent with web search to verify individual facts in long-form responses. Similarly, SAGE ( 4 ) employs a tool-augmented agent that iteratively retrieves and synthesizes external evidence for reference-free QA evaluation. These works improve judge accuracy but provide no formal guarantee on the reliability of verdicts. Uncertainty quantification for LLM evaluation. Existing methods generally fall into two categories. White-box methods estimate uncertainty from the judge’s token probabilities. The most common choice is the predictive entropy of the output distribution ( 20 ) . These probabilities are often well calibrated with respect to correctness ( 16 ) . Black-box methods, in contrast, estimate uncertainty by querying the judge repeatedly and measuring how consistent its verdicts are ( 31 ; 32 ) . Both signals correlate with judge accuracy and can flag low-confidence verdicts ( 5 ) . However, they remain heuristic. For instance, a threshold chosen by hand or tuned on a validation set gives no formal guarantee on the error rate among accepted verdicts. Uncertainty-based routing and tool use. A parallel line of work uses uncertainty to determine when additional resources are needed. FrugalGPT ( 8 ) and AutoMix ( 1 ) use confidence to route queries across models with different capabilities, trading off cost against quality. In contrast, FLARE ( 13 ) uses token-level uncertainty to decide when to retrieve external information during generation. More recently, SAGE ( 4 ) introduced search-augmented retrieval for LLM judges, where the judge acts as an agent that gathers targeted evidence when evaluating free-form answers. However, these approaches often rely on unconditional retrieval, which introduces unnecessary computation. Furthermore, they do not provide formal guarantees on the error rate of the resulting evaluations. Risk-controlled selective evaluation. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free, finite-sample coverage guarantees by constructing prediction sets calibrated on held-out data ( 2 ) . Conformal risk control generalizes this beyond coverage to bound arbitrary loss functions, including the FDR, at user-specified levels ( 3 ) . Recent work has applied these guarantees to question answering. SConU builds prediction sets that cover admissible answers with high probability ( 34 ) . Similarly, COIN ( 33 ) calibrates an uncertainty threshold that bounds the FDR among accepted answers using Clopper–Pearson upper confidence bounds ( 10 ) . Closer to our setting, Trust or Escalate ( 15 ) and SCOPE ( 5 ) adapt risk-controlled selective prediction to pairwise evaluation and provide guarantee on human agreement among accepted judgments. However, both target subjective preference tasks where the judge compares two responses rather than evaluating factual correctness (i.e., objective evaluation). Our framework introduces risk-controlled retrieval-augmented evaluation, where retrieval is selectively activated based on calibrated uncertainty thresholds. Unlike unconditional retrieval approaches, it provides formal FDR guarantees for the accepted verdicts. 3 Methodology We propose a risk-controlled framework for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. The framework calibrates uncertainty thresholds on a held-out set with human labels so that, among all instances the judge evaluates, the probability of producing an incorrect verdict is bounded by a user-specified risk level α \alpha ( 2 ; 3 ) . evidence.title: Sequential Design and Spatial Modeling for Portfolio Tail Risk Measurement
evidence.excerpt: We consider calculation of capital requirements when the underlying economic scenarios are determined by simulatable risk factors. In the respective nested simulation framework, the goal is to estimate portfolio tail risk, quantified via VaR or TVaR of a given collection of future economic scenarios representing factor levels at the risk horizon. Traditionally, evaluating portfolio losses of an outer scenario is done by computing a conditional expectation via inner-level Monte Carlo and is computationally expensive. We introduce several inter-related machine learning techniques to speed up this computation, in particular by properly accounting for the simulation noise. Our main workhorse is an advanced Gaussian Process (GP) regression approach which uses nonparametric spatial modeling to efficiently learn the relationship between the stochastic factors defining scenarios and corresponding portfolio value. Leveraging this emulator, we develop sequential algorithms that adaptively allocate inner simulation budgets to target the quantile region. The GP framework also yields better uncertainty quantification for the resulting VaR/TVaR estimators that reduces bias and variance compared to existing methods. We illustrate the proposed strategies with two case-studies in two and six dimensions.

evidence.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Uncertainty-Aware and Abstention-Enabled Acute Ischemic Stroke Imaging Decisions
evidence.excerpt: Artificial intelligence models have shown strong potential in acute ischemic stroke imaging, particularly for lesion detection and segmentation using computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. However, most existing approaches operate as black box predictors, producing deterministic outputs without explicit uncertainty awareness or structured mechanisms to abstain under ambiguous conditions. This limitation raises serious safety and trust concerns in high risk emergency radiology settings. In this paper, we propose an explainable agentic AI framework for uncertainty aware and abstention enabled decision support in acute ischemic stroke imaging. The framework follows a modular agentic pipeline in which a perception agent performs lesion aware image analysis, an uncertainty estimation agent computes slice level predictive reliability, and a decision agent determines whether to issue a prediction or abstain based on predefined uncertainty thresholds. Unlike prior stroke imaging systems that primarily focus on improving segmentation or classification accuracy, the proposed framework explicitly prioritizes clinical safety, transparency, and clinician aligned decision behavior. Qualitative and case based analyses across representative stroke imaging scenarios demonstrate that uncertainty driven abstention naturally emerges in diagnostically ambiguous regions and low information slices. The framework further integrates visual explanation mechanisms to support both predictive and abstention decisions, addressing a key limitation of existing uncertainty aware medical imaging systems. Rather than introducing a new performance benchmark, this work presents agentic control, uncertainty awareness, and selective abstention as essential design principles for developing safe and trustworthy medical imaging AI systems.

evidence.title: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain: Uncertainty-Guarded LLM Judging with Provable Risk Guarantees
evidence.excerpt: Using LLMs as judges has become standard practice for evaluating model outputs at scale. This is particularly common for subjective, open-ended tasks such as assessing helpfulness or alignment, where no single reference answer exists. However, objective tasks introduce a distinct reliability challenge for reference-free LLM judging. In the absence of a reference answer, the judge evaluates factual correctness either through its parametric knowledge or through tool augmentation. Although the former enables efficient evaluation, the judge may hallucinate or lack sufficient evidence for its verdict. Conversely, tool augmentation can provide additional evidence but introduces extra computational cost and requires an appropriate mechanism to determine when and how that evidence should be used reliably. More importantly, neither approach alone provides formal control over the risk of accepted verdicts or guarantees their reliability at a specified level. We propose a risk-controlled framework that calibrates uncertainty thresholds on a held-out set so that the false discovery rate among accepted verdicts remains below a user-specified level~$α$ with high probability, using finite-sample Clopper--Pearson intervals. When the parametric mode is not sufficiently confident, the instance is routed to a retrieval-augmented mode, where the judge gathers web evidence and re-evaluates the instance under a second calibrated threshold. The finite-sample guarantee carries over to this two-threshold routing without additional assumptions. Across open-domain QA benchmarks and judges of varying scales, the framework maintains the target error rate while achieving substantially higher coverage than single-mode baselines.

evidence.title: Reassessing Extractive QA Datasets at Scale: LLM-as-a-Judge and In-Depth Analyses
evidence.excerpt: Extractive QA tasks are commonly evaluated using Exact Match (EM) and F1-score, but these metrics often fail to reflect true model performance. Recent studies have proposed using large language models (LLMs) as judges (LLM-as-a-judge), yet they often lack comprehensive evaluation across datasets and overlook key factors such as sensitivity to answer types, prompt variations, and self-preference bias. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of LLM-as-a-judge across four extractive QA datasets and various prompt variations, assessing multiple LLM families in both answering and judging roles. Our results show that LLM-as-a-judge judgments correlate much more strongly with human evaluations than EM (0.22) and F1 (0.40), achieving correlations up to 0.85 with open-source models. Further analysis reveals that LLM-as-a-judge performs particularly well on number-related answers but faces challenges with more complex types, such as job titles. Contrary to findings in other NLP tasks, we observe no self-preference bias, even when the same model serves as both QA model and judge. Finally, we find that prompt phrasing has minimal impact, and zero-shot, context-free judging often yields the best evaluation performance.

evidence.title: Can LLM be a Personalized Judge?
evidence.excerpt: Ensuring that large language models (LLMs) reflect diverse user values and preferences is crucial as their user bases expand globally. It is therefore encouraging to see the growing interest in LLM personalization within the research community. However, current works often rely on the LLM-as-a-Judge approach for evaluation without thoroughly examining its validity. In this paper, we investigate the reliability of LLM-as-a-Personalized-Judge, asking LLMs to judge user preferences based on personas. Our findings suggest that directly applying LLM-as-a-Personalized-Judge is less reliable than previously assumed, showing low and inconsistent agreement with human ground truth. The personas typically used are often overly simplistic, resulting in low predictive power. To address these issues, we introduce verbal uncertainty estimation into the LLM-as-a-Personalized-Judge pipeline, allowing the model to express low confidence on uncertain judgments. This adjustment leads to much higher agreement (above 80%) on high-certainty samples for binary tasks. Through human evaluation, we find that the LLM-as-a-Personalized-Judge achieves comparable performance to third-party humans evaluation and even surpasses human performance on high-certainty samples. Our work indicates that certainty-enhanced LLM-as-a-Personalized-Judge offers a promising direction for developing more reliable and scalable methods for evaluating LLM personalization.

evidence.title: A generic nonparametric value-at-risk estimator for high dimensions
evidence.excerpt: We present in this article a non-parametric value-at-risk (VaR+CVaR) algorithm that remains accurate for an arbitrarily large number of underlying positions. The algorithm solves the two inherent problems of VaR estimation. First, past history is not directly applicable to the future, but all predictions of the future are based on the past. Second, VaR estimation is equivalent to modeling a single corner of a high-dimensional space (the corner where all bets lose simultaneously). The algorithm only uses mathematical methods that strictly do not degrade in accuracy at high-dimensions. Historical data are then directly incorporated with all high-dimensional relationships present, without manipulation. We test the algorithm with an ensemble of 500 portfolios with random positions across 49 distinct liquid futures of different expiries (VIX, equity indexes, gov. bonds, rates, energy, metals, livestock, agriculture, and softs). All VaR estimations are performed strictly blind to the future. The median portfolio rate of loss exceeding the 99% confidence daily VaR estimate is between $1.0\pm0.1$% depending on algorithm input parameters. 68% of portfolios have a rate of loss exceeding 99% VaR between $1.0\pm0.3$%, and 95% of portfolios between $1.0\pm0.5$%.

evidence.title: Analyzing Uncertainty of LLM-as-a-Judge: Interval Evaluations with Conformal Prediction
evidence.excerpt: LLM-as-a-judge has become a promising paradigm for using large language models (LLMs) to evaluate natural language generation (NLG), but the uncertainty of its evaluation remains underexplored. This lack of reliability may limit its deployment in many applications. This work presents the first framework to analyze the uncertainty by offering a prediction interval of LLM-based scoring via conformal prediction. Conformal prediction constructs continuous prediction intervals from a single evaluation run, and we design an ordinal boundary adjustment for discrete rating tasks. We also suggest a midpoint-based score within the interval as a low-bias alternative to raw model score and weighted average. We perform extensive experiments and analysis, which show that conformal prediction can provide valid prediction interval with coverage guarantees. We also explore the usefulness of interval midpoint and judge reprompting for better judgment.

evidence.title: Statistical Emulators for Pricing and Hedging Longevity Risk Products
evidence.excerpt: We propose the use of statistical emulators for the purpose of valuing mortality-linked contracts in stochastic mortality models. Such models typically require (nested) evaluation of expected values of nonlinear functionals of multi-dimensional stochastic processes. Except in the simplest cases, no closed-form expressions are available, necessitating numerical approximation. Rather than building ad hoc analytic approximations, we advocate the use of modern statistical tools from machine learning to generate a flexible, non-parametric surrogate for the true mappings. This method allows performance guarantees regarding approximation accuracy and removes the need for nested simulation. We illustrate our approach with case studies involving (i) a Lee-Carter model with mortality shocks, (ii) index-based static hedging with longevity basis risk; (iii) a Cairns-Blake-Dowd stochastic survival probability model.

evidence.title: On the Selection of Loss Severity Distributions to Model Operational Risk
evidence.excerpt: Accurate modeling of operational risk is important for a bank and the finance industry as a whole to prepare for potentially catastrophic losses. One approach to modeling operational is the loss distribution approach, which requires a bank to group operational losses into risk categories and select a loss frequency and severity distribution for each category. This approach estimates the annual operational loss distribution, and a bank must set aside capital, called regulatory capital, equal to the 0.999 quantile of this estimated distribution. In practice, this approach may produce unstable regulatory capital calculations from year-to-year as selected loss severity distribution families change. This paper presents truncation probability estimates for loss severity data and a consistent quantile scoring function on annual loss data as useful severity distribution selection criteria that may lead to more stable regulatory capital. Additionally, the Sinh-arcSinh distribution is another flexible candidate family for modeling loss severities that can be easily estimated using the maximum likelihood approach. Finally, we recommend that loss frequencies below the minimum reporting threshold be collected so that loss severity data can be treated as censored data.

evidence.title: Evaluating Range Value at Risk Forecasts
evidence.excerpt: The debate of what quantitative risk measure to choose in practice has mainly focused on the dichotomy between Value at Risk (VaR) -- a quantile -- and Expected Shortfall (ES) -- a tail expectation. Range Value at Risk (RVaR) is a natural interpolation between these two prominent risk measures, which constitutes a tradeoff between the sensitivity of the latter and the robustness of the former, turning it into a practically relevant risk measure on its own. As such, there is a need to statistically validate RVaR forecasts and to compare and rank the performance of different RVaR models, tasks subsumed under the term 'backtesting' in finance. The predictive performance is best evaluated and compared in terms of strictly consistent loss or scoring functions. That is, functions which are minimised in expectation by the correct RVaR forecast. Much like ES, it has been shown recently that RVaR does not admit strictly consistent scoring functions, i.e., it is not elicitable. Mitigating this negative result, this paper shows that a triplet of RVaR with two VaR components at different levels is elicitable. We characterise the class of strictly consistent scoring functions for this triplet. Additional properties of these scoring functions are examined, including the diagnostic tool of Murphy diagrams. The results are illustrated with a simulation study, and we put our approach in perspective with respect to the classical approach of trimmed least squares in robust regression.

evidence.title: Conformal Risk Control
evidence.excerpt: We extend conformal prediction to control the expected value of any monotone loss function. The algorithm generalizes split conformal prediction together with its coverage guarantee. Like conformal prediction, the conformal risk control procedure is tight up to an $\mathcal{O}(1/n)$ factor. We also introduce extensions of the idea to distribution shift, quantile risk control, multiple and adversarial risk control, and expectations of U-statistics. Worked examples from computer vision and natural language processing demonstrate the usage of our algorithm to bound the false negative rate, graph distance, and token-level F1-score.

evidence.title: Explicit Abstention Knobs for Predictable Reliability in Video Question Answering
evidence.excerpt: High-stakes deployment of vision-language models (VLMs) requires selective prediction, where systems abstain when uncertain rather than risk costly errors. We investigate whether confidence-based abstention provides reliable control over error rates in video question answering, and whether that control remains robust under distribution shift. Using NExT-QA and Gemini 2.0 Flash, we establish two findings. First, confidence thresholding provides mechanistic control in-distribution. Sweeping threshold epsilon produces smooth risk-coverage tradeoffs, reducing error rates f

evidence.title: FinPT: Financial Risk Prediction with Profile Tuning on Pretrained Foundation Models
evidence.excerpt: Financial risk prediction plays a crucial role in the financial sector. Machine learning methods have been widely applied for automatically detecting potential risks and thus saving the cost of labor. However, the development in this field is lagging behind in recent years by the following two facts: 1) the algorithms used are somewhat outdated, especially in the context of the fast advance of generative AI and large language models (LLMs); 2) the lack of a unified and open-sourced financial benchmark has impeded the related research for years. To tackle these issues, we propose FinPT and FinBench: the former is a novel approach for financial risk prediction that conduct Profile Tuning on large pretrained foundation models, and the latter is a set of high-quality datasets on financial risks such as default, fraud, and churn. In FinPT, we fill the financial tabular data into the pre-defined instruction template, obtain natural-language customer profiles by prompting LLMs, and fine-tune large foundation models with the profile text to make predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed FinPT by experimenting with a range of representative strong baselines on FinBench. The analytical studies further deepen the understanding of LLMs for financial risk prediction.

evidence.title: A Framework for Time-Consistent, Risk-Sensitive Model Predictive Control: Theory and Algorithms
evidence.excerpt: In this paper we present a framework for risk-sensitive model predictive control (MPC) of linear systems affected by stochastic multiplicative uncertainty. Our key innovation is to consider a time-consistent, dynamic risk evaluation of the cumulative cost as the objective function to be minimized. This framework is axiomatically justified in terms of time-consistency of risk assessments, is amenable to dynamic optimization, and is unifying in the sense that it captures a full range of risk preferences from risk-neutral (i.e., expectation) to worst case. Within this framework, we propose and analyze an online risk-sensitive MPC algorithm that is provably stabilizing. Furthermore, by exploiting the dual representation of time-consistent, dynamic risk measures, we cast the computation of the MPC control law as a convex optimization problem amenable to real-time implementation. Simulation results are presented and discussed.

evidence.title: Individual risk in mean-field control models for decentralized control, with application to automated demand response
evidence.excerpt: Flexibility of energy consumption can be harnessed for the purposes of ancillary services in a large power grid. In prior work by the authors a randomized control architecture is introduced for individual loads for this purpose. In examples it is shown that the control architecture can be designed so that control of the loads is easy at the grid level: Tracking of a balancing authority reference signal is possible, while ensuring that the quality of service (QoS) for each load is acceptable on average. The analysis was based on a mean field limit (as the number of loads approaches infinity), combined with an LTI-system approximation of the aggregate nonlinear model. This paper examines in depth the issue of individual risk in these systems. The main contributions of the paper are of two kinds: Risk is modeled and quantified: (i) The average performance is not an adequate measure of success. It is found empirically that a histogram of QoS is approximately Gaussian, and consequently each load will eventually receive poor service. (ii) The variance can be estimated from a refinement of the LTI model that includes a white-noise disturbance; variance is a function of the randomized policy, as well as the power spectral density of the reference signal. Additional local control can eliminate risk: (iii) The histogram of QoS is truncated through this local control, so that strict bounds on service quality are guaranteed. (iv) This has insignificant impact on the grid-level performance, beyond a modest reduction in capacity of ancillary service.

evidence.title: Monte Carlo uncertainty estimation for wavelength calibration
evidence.excerpt: CIPM published the Supplement I for GUM in 2008 as not only an alternative approach to estimate the uncertainty for a given calibration measurement but also as a proper uncertainty estimation one, whenever any of the conditions imposed in GUM which must be satisfied does not hold [1, 2]. Before the introduction of the new approach in the Supplement I, namely Monte Carlo (MC) method, the GUM rules have been always applied even if in cases where the mentioned conditions were not fulfilled. After or even before the official introduction of this MC method, a number of published papers in uncertainty estimation by using MC method had been shown up, giving more insight for the ways the uncertainties estimated and also for the specific calibration measurements under investigation themselves [3 - 16]. However, in most of those published papers, the application conditions required before a method selection should be analyzed, in fact, has been ignored. In our uncertainty study for wavelength calibration by using beat frequency technique, the application conditions have not been ignored but analyzed carefully and it was found that a GUM application condition was unsatisfactory. However, all the MC method conditions for this calibration problem have been well fulfilled. A computer program was then coded [17] following the steps in the Supplement I. The resultant outputs showed difference in statistical nature and suggested to replace the MC method to the GUM one as soon as possible for this case.

evidence.title: Can LLMs Replace Human Evaluators? An Empirical Study of LLM-as-a-Judge in Software Engineering
evidence.excerpt: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been deployed to tackle various software engineering (SE) tasks like code generation, significantly advancing the automation of SE tasks. However, assessing the quality of these LLM-generated code and text remains challenging. The commonly used Pass@k metric necessitates extensive unit tests and configured environments, demands a high labor cost, and is not suitable for evaluating LLM-generated text. Conventional metrics like BLEU, which measure only lexical rather than semantic similarity, have also come under scrutiny. In response, a new trend has emerged to employ LLMs for automated evaluation, known as LLM-as-a-judge. These LLM-as-a-judge methods are claimed to better mimic human assessment than conventional metrics without relying on high-quality reference answers. Nevertheless, their exact human alignment in SE tasks remains unexplored. In this paper, we empirically explore LLM-as-a-judge methods for evaluating SE tasks, focusing on their alignment with human judgments. We select seven LLM-as-a-judge methods that utilize general-purpose LLMs, alongside two LLMs specifically fine-tuned for evaluation. After generating and manually scoring LLM responses on three recent SE datasets of code translation, code generation, and code summarization, we then prompt these methods to evaluate each response. Finally, we compare the scores generated by these methods with human evaluation. The results indicate that output-based methods reach the highest Pearson correlation of 81.32 and 68.51 with human scores in code translation and generation, achieving near-human evaluation, noticeably outperforming ChrF++, one of the best conventional metrics, at 34.23 and 64.92. Such output-based methods prompt LLMs to output judgments directly, and exhibit more balanced score distributions that resemble human score patterns. Finally, we provide...

evidence.title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
evidence.excerpt: Accurate and consistent evaluation is crucial for decision-making across numerous fields, yet it remains a challenging task due to inherent subjectivity, variability, and scale. Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, leading to the emergence of "LLM-as-a-Judge," where LLMs are employed as evaluators for complex tasks. With their ability to process diverse data types and provide scalable, cost-effective, and consistent assessments, LLMs present a compelling alternative to traditional expert-driven evaluations. However, ensuring the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems remains a significant challenge that requires careful design and standardization. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of LLM-as-a-Judge, addressing the core question: How can reliable LLM-as-a-Judge systems be built? We explore strategies to enhance reliability, including improving consistency, mitigating biases, and adapting to diverse assessment scenarios. Additionally, we propose methodologies for evaluating the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems, supported by a novel benchmark designed for this purpose. To advance the development and real-world deployment of LLM-as-a-Judge systems, we also discussed practical applications, challenges, and future directions. This survey serves as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners in this rapidly evolving field.

evidence.title: Systematic Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge in LLM Alignment Tasks: Explainable Metrics and Diverse Prompt Templates
evidence.excerpt: LLM-as-a-Judge has been widely applied to evaluate and compare different LLM alignmnet approaches (e.g., RLHF and DPO). However, concerns regarding its reliability have emerged, due to LLM judges' biases and inconsistent decision-making. Previous research has developed evaluation frameworks to assess reliability of LLM judges and their alignment with human preferences. However, the employed evaluation metrics often lack adequate explainability and fail to address LLM internal inconsistency. Additionally, existing studies inadequately explore the impact of various prompt templates when applying LLM-as-a-Judge methods, leading to potentially inconsistent comparisons between different alignment algorithms. In this work, we systematically evaluate LLM-as-a-Judge on alignment tasks by defining more theoretically interpretable evaluation metrics and explicitly mitigating LLM internal inconsistency from reliability metrics. We develop an open-source framework to evaluate, compare, and visualize the reliability and alignment of LLM judges, which facilitates practitioners to choose LLM judges for alignment tasks. In the experiments, we examine effects of diverse prompt templates on LLM-judge reliability and also demonstrate our developed framework by comparing various LLM judges on two common alignment datasets (i.e., TL;DR Summarization and HH-RLHF-Helpfulness). Our results indicate a significant impact of prompt templates on LLM judge performance, as well as a mediocre alignment level between the tested LLM judges and human evaluators.

evidence.title: Propagation of Linear Uncertainties through Multiline Thru-Reflect-Line Calibration
evidence.excerpt: This study proposes a linear approach for propagating uncertainties in the multiline thru-reflect-line (TRL) calibration method for vector network analyzers. The multiline TRL formulation we are proposing applies the law of uncertainty propagation as outlined in the ISO Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM) to both measurement and model uncertainties. In addition, we conducted a Monte Carlo analysis using a combination of measured and synthetic data to model various uncertainties, such as additive noise, reflect asymmetry, line mismatch, and line length offset. The results of our linear uncertainty formulation demonstrate agreement with the Monte Carlo method and provide a more efficient means of assessing the uncertainty budget of the multiline TRL calibration.

evidence.title: Permutation-Consensus Listwise Judging for Robust Factuality Evaluation
evidence.excerpt: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used as judges, yet their decisions can change under presentation choices that should be irrelevant. We study one such source of instability: candidate-order sensitivity in listwise factuality evaluation, where several answers can look similarly polished while differing substantially in hallucination risk. We introduce PCFJudge, an inference-time method that reruns the same factuality-first listwise prompt over multiple orderings of the same candidate set and aggregates the resulting scores, ranks, and uncertainty signals into a single consensus decision. On RewardBench 2 Factuality, the final seven-permutation aggregate (K=7) improves top-1 selection accuracy from 86.00% to 91.33% with GPT-5.4 and from 86.33% to 89.67% with Claude Sonnet 4.6. These results suggest that candidate order can be a meaningful source of factuality-judging error and that marginalizing over this nuisance variation can improve the reliability of LLM evaluation.

evidence.title: Analyzing Uncertainty of LLM-as-a-Judge: Interval Evaluations with Conformal Prediction
evidence.excerpt: Analyzing Uncertainty of LLM-as-a-Judge: Interval Evaluations with Conformal Prediction Huanxin Sheng Xinyi Liu Hangfeng He Jieyu Zhao Jian Kang Affiliation: University of Rochester, University of Southern California, MBZUAI {hsheng2@ur., hangfeng.he@, xinyu.liu1@simon.}rochester.edujieyuz@usc.edu, jian.kang@mbzuai.ac.ae Abstract LLM-as-a-judge has become a promising paradigm for using large language models (LLMs) to evaluate natural language generation (NLG), but the uncertainty of its evaluation remains underexplored. This lack of reliability may limit its deployment in many applications. This work presents the first framework to analyze the uncertainty by offering a prediction interval of LLM-based scoring via conformal prediction. Conformal prediction constructs continuous prediction intervals from a single evaluation run, and we design an ordinal boundary adjustment for discrete rating tasks. We also suggest a midpoint-based score within the interval as a low-bias alternative to raw model score and weighted average. We perform extensive experiments and analysis, which show that conformal prediction can provide valid prediction interval with coverage guarantees. We also explore the usefulness of interval midpoint and judge reprompting for better judgment. 1 1 1 Our code and data are available at https://github.com/BruceSheng1202/Analyzing_Uncertainty_of_LLM-as-a-Judge 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have become powerful automatic evaluators for natural language generation (NLG) tasks, known as LLM-as-a-judge. Its consistency with human judgments results in strong performance with respect to metrics like ROUGE ( Lin 2004 ) , BLEU ( Papineni et al. 2002 ) , and BERTScore ( Zhang et al. 2020 ) . Besides, LLM judges can flexibly adapt to diverse evaluation criteria and provide scalable, cost-effective assessments compared to expert annotation ( Gao et al. 2024 ; Gu et al. 2025 ) . These advantages make the LLM-as-a-judge useful in various scenarios, such as clinical radiology ( Chaves et al. 2024 ) , rumor detection ( Hong et al. 2025 ) , cyberattack detection ( Yong et al. 2025 ) and wildlife trafficking identification ( Barbosa et al. 2025 ) . However, a single evaluation from a LLM judge might be biased ( Wu and Aji 2023 ; Li et al. 2024c ) and uncertain due to inherent randomness ( Schroeder and Wood-Doughty 2024 ) , thus undermining its reliability in scenarios like healthcare ( Chung et al. 2025 ) and finance ( Kamble et al. 2025 ) . Though a LLM judge can express its confidence with well-designed prompt or via fine-tuning ( Xu et al. 2024a ; Liu et al. 2024 ; Taubenfeld et al. 2025 ) , it may still suffer from overconfidence ( Xiong et al. 2024 ) or dishonesty ( Li et al. 2024e ) . We ask: How can a LLM judge provide reliable evaluation given the user request? Conformal prediction ( Vovk et al. 2005 ) is a promising way to quantify the uncertainty of an LLM judge ( Ye et al. 2024 ) . It outputs a prediction interval (or set for classification) to a model output with three key advantages. First, conformal prediction is a distribution-free uncertainty quantification method, which is suitable for black-box models like LLMs due to unknown input data distribution for most (if not all) LLMs. Second, it can provide post-hoc uncertainty quantification using only a calibration step based on LLM outputs. Third, the prediction interval given by conformal prediction enjoys statistically guaranteed coverage, i.e., how likely the ground truth falls within the interval, as long as the data is exchangeable. In this paper, we comprehensively evaluate nine 2 2 2 Seven regression-type and two ordinal-type methods. conformal prediction methods in quantifying the uncertainty of a LLM judge in rating-based evaluation tasks, each of which constructs a prediction interval for a rating output by the LLM judge. For each conformal prediction method, we evaluate its efficiency (i.e., average width of prediction intervals) and coverage (i.e., the probability that ground truths fall within prediction intervals). Furthermore, to adapt to the ordinal and discrete nature in organic rating-based evaluation, we propose boundary adjustment that adjusts the endpoints of prediction interval to be aligned with the rating scales. We prove that the boundary adjustment yields an interval suitable to the ordinal setting with provable non-decreasing coverage. From our comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that the quality of prediction interval attributes to design choices of the LLM judge (e.g., which LLM to use as the judge, which prompting strategy for evaluation) as well as the size of calibration data during calibration. Finally, we show that the midpoint of the prediction interval provides better estimate to the ground truth to further assist better decision-making, while reprompting the LLM judge with prediction interval might not improve the judgement. Our analysis advocate for a shift from direct scoring to uncertainty-aware evaluations, offering references for more reliable evaluation and better decision-making. In summary, our contributions are • To our knowledge, we are the first to analyze the uncertainty of LLM-as-a-judge using conformal prediction in rating-based evaluation. • We design boundary adjustment to improve the efficiency empirically without compromising the coverage. The interval midpoints suggest better alignment to human evaluation. • We analyze factors affecting the interval quality, including the LLM-as-a-judge framework itself, the choice of LLM in the framework, and the size of calibration in conformal prediction, and offer practical insights or recommended choices. 2 Related Work Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-as-a-Judge. Uncertainty quantification for LLM-as-a-judge is an important yet less explored area. Wagner et al. 2024 prompt the judge to justify each rating option as if it were correct and then construct a confusion matrix from token-level probabilities of these assessments to derive confidence scores. Xie et al. 2025 use token probabilities to estimate the confidence of judgments, and demonstrate that such measures exhibit bias and instability through extensive experiments. Similar conclusions are also found when applying other two common paradigms: (1) prompting LLMs to self-report confidence ( Yona et al. 2024 ; Xu et al. 2024a ) , which can suffer from overconfidence ( Xiong et al. 2024 ) or dishonesty ( Li et al. 2024e ) , and (2) consistency-based approaches that rely on multiple generations ( Tian et al. 2023 ; Xiong et al. 2024 ) , which, like the confusion matrix-based method, are computationally expensive. To our best knowledge, Jung et al. 2024 is the most relevant work to us, which applies conformalized risk control ( Angelopoulos et al. 2022b ) to ensure agreement with human preferences in pairwise response comparison ( Zhou et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2024b ; Li et al. 2024d ; Zhang et al. 2025 ; van den Burg et al. 2025 ) . In contrast, we focus on using conformal prediction to quantify uncertainty in rating tasks instead of pairwise preference modeling. evidence.excerpt: We introduce a framework for calibrating machine learning models so that their predictions satisfy explicit, finite-sample statistical guarantees. Our calibration algorithms work with any underlying model and (unknown) data-generating distribution and do not require model refitting. The framework addresses, among other examples, false discovery rate control in multi-label classification, intersection-over-union control in instance segmentation, and the simultaneous control of the type-1 error of outlier detection and confidence set coverage in classification or regression. Our main insight is to reframe the risk-control problem as multiple hypothesis testing, enabling techniques and mathematical arguments different from those in the previous literature. We use the framework to provide new calibration methods for several core machine learning tasks, with detailed worked examples in computer vision and tabular medical data.

Jordan Lihua Lei August 11, 2026 Abstract We introduce a framework for calibrating machine learning models so that their predictions satisfy explicit, finite-sample statistical guarantees. Our calibration algorithms work with any underlying model and (unknown) data-generating distribution and do not require model refitting. The framework addresses, among other examples, false discovery rate control in multi-label classification, intersection-over-union control in instance segmentation, and the simultaneous control of the type-1 error of outlier detection and confidence set coverage in classification or regression. Our main insight is to reframe the risk-control problem as multiple hypothesis testing, enabling techniques and mathematical arguments different from those in the previous literature. We use the framework to provide new calibration methods for several core machine learning tasks, with detailed worked examples in computer vision and tabular medical data. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Object detection with simultaneous distribution-free guarantees on the expected intersection-over-union, recall, and coverage rate is possible with our methods; see Section 4 for details. Deep neural networks and other complex machine learning models are increasingly used in real-world systems. Their use is motivated by the fact that (a) they often give the best prediction accuracy and (b) they extend to prediction tasks with structured outputs, such as image segmentation, predicting 3D volumes, sentence completion, and so on. However, the standard statistical toolbox does not apply to these models, so users seeking assurances about the reliability of predictions, such as bounds on the false discovery rate across multiple decisions, are left without recourse. For example, the Facebook object detector we used to produce Figure 1 is currently deployed without any rigorous notion of uncertainty. Knowing when and how badly a model is likely to fail is critical for safe deployment; we urgently need new statistical tools for this task. We develop a tool to endow complex prediction models with statistical guarantees. Our proposed Learn then Test (LTT) framework and bestows finite-sample guarantees on any predictive model, without assumptions on the inner workings of the model or the true distribution underlying the dataset. Our approach is modular in this sense, allowing it to keep pace with the ever-evolving ecosystem of neural network architectures, fitting schemes, and data types. In LTT, we begin with a learned model f ^ \hat{f} . We then post-process the model using calibration data in order to make our final predictions. The post-processing is controlled by a low-dimensional parameter λ \lambda . We test multiple values of the parameter using the calibration data in order to find settings that control a user-chosen statistical error rate. Thus, we link the problem of distribution-free predictive inference with the well-developed ideas in multiple hypothesis testing in order to ensure the reliability of machine learning models. As an example, a multi-label classification model f ^ : 𝒳 → [ 0 , 1 ] K \hat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]^{K} generally outputs the estimated probability that each of K K classes is in an image. The parameter λ \lambda is the binarization threshold that determines which classes we include in the prediction 𝒯 λ ​ ( x ) = { k : f ^ ​ ( x ) k ≥ λ } \mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(x)=\{k:\hat{f}(x)_{k}\geq\lambda\} . We apply our technique to this problem in Section 3.1 , and also to four other core problems in machine learning: selective classification, selective regression, out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, and instance segmentation. The resulting guarantees are the first of their kind; all previous work in distribution-free uncertainty quantification, such as conformal prediction [ 1 ] and risk-controlling prediction sets [ 2 ] , have required that λ \lambda is one-dimensional and that the risk function be monotonic in λ \lambda . We do not make these assumptions, and can thus control many possibly non-monotone risks. This approach dates back at least to tolerance regions (sets that cover a pre-specified fraction of the population distribution) in the 1940s [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . See [ 7 ] for a review of this topic. Recently, tolerance regions have been used to form prediction sets with deep learning models [ 8 , 9 ] . In parallel, conformal prediction [ 10 , 1 , 11 ] has been developed as a way to produce prediction sets with finite-sample statistical guarantees. One convenient, widely-used form of conformal prediction, known as split conformal prediction [ 12 , 13 ] , uses data splitting to generate prediction sets in a computationally efficient way; see also [ 14 , 15 ] for generalizations that re-use data for improved statistical efficiency.
